changes.after: Give each enum case a fixed number and check numbers safely.

before: A raw value is a fixed value attached to each enum case. Here each Priority case has one distinct Int code. This differs from an associated value: an associated value can carry different data each time a case is constructed. Raw values let you convert a known case to a code and attempt the reverse conversion safely.

Priority.high.rawValue reads 8. Priority(rawValue: raw) uses a synthesized failable initializer and returns Priority?; not every Int is a valid code. guard let unwraps a recognized case or returns "unknown". switch handles all three cases, so no fallback case is needed for an already valid Priority. The leading dot uses the known enum type.

Follow this complete example.
```swift
enum Priority: Int {
    case low = 1
    case normal = 4
    case high = 8
}
func priorityText(_ raw: Int) -> String {
    guard let value = Priority(rawValue: raw) else {
        return "unknown"
    }
    switch value {
    case .low: return "low"
    case .normal: return "normal"
    case .high: return "high"
    }
}
print(Priority.high.rawValue)
print(priorityText(4))
print(priorityText(5))
```
Output:
```text
8
normal
unknown
```

after: An enum's raw value is a fixed code attached to one of its cases. Priority uses 1 for low, 4 for normal, and 8 for high. Unlike an associated value, this code stays the same every time you use that case.

Priority.high.rawValue reads its code. Priority(rawValue: raw) tries to find a case with the supplied code. The result may be nil, meaning no case matches. guard let continues only when a match exists.
A raw-value lookup needs an exact match. It does not round to the nearest code or create a new case. After a match is found, switch chooses the name of that case.
